title: Bread Lab
goal: Your kid finds out that bread is alive before it's food. They wake yeast in cold, warm and hot water, feed it and watch it blow up a balloon, knead dough until it stretches thin as a window, measure the rise, then bake a real loaf and use baker's math to scale it for the whole family.
need: About 600 g of flour, salt, a little sugar and 3 packets of dry yeast (or a small jar)
A kitchen scale, 3 cups and 3 small bottles
3 balloons if you have them, or 3 clear glasses instead
A tall straight glass, tape, a ruler and an oven

academics.subject: Science
academics.text: yeast is alive: it eats sugar and makes gas

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: weighing, measuring the rise and baker's percentages

academics.subject: Life skills
academics.text: baking a real loaf from scratch

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Bread rewards patience more than skill, so pick a slow day at home. Handle the oven and the hot water yourself, let them get their hands in the dough, and keep asking what they think the yeast is doing right now.

plan.what: Wake the yeast and set up the balloon test (Steps 1 and 2).
Mix, knead, then measure the rise (Steps 3 and 4).
Shape, rise again, bake, slice and scale (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: The yeast may be old, or the water too hot. Try a fresh packet and water that feels like a warm bath on the inside of your wrist.

troubleshoot.q: The dough is too sticky to knead
troubleshoot.a: Keep kneading for a few minutes before adding flour. It usually gets smoother on its own. Add flour a spoonful at a time only if it doesn't.

troubleshoot.q: The loaf came out flat and heavy
troubleshoot.a: Good data. Ask what was different: shorter kneading, a cold kitchen, less rise time. Change one thing next time.

lesson.text: Yeast is a tiny living thing. Give it warm water and something to eat, and it makes gas, like bubbles. Kneading builds stretchy strands in the dough that trap those bubbles, and that's what makes bread rise.
lesson.before: 'Bread just puffs up in the oven.'

model.line: A thick layer of foam that smells like bread.
Nothing at all, even after an hour.
Yeast is alive. Too cold and it's slow, too hot and it dies.

lesson.modelNote: 'It just puffs up' had nothing living in it. Three cups side by side showed the yeast waking up, and the hot one that never foamed showed it could die.

steps.title: Wake the yeast
steps.why: Yeast looks like dust. The first test shows it's alive, and what it needs.
steps.kid: Your kid puts a teaspoon of yeast and a pinch of sugar in three cups, then adds cold, warm and very hot water, using the Yeast test card in the Bread Lab Toolkit at the end of the guide. They guess first, then check every 5 minutes.
steps.you: Pour the very hot water yourself, from a kettle that has cooled for a minute. Ask them to write their guess before anything happens.
ask: Which cup do you think will foam first?
Why do you think the hot one didn't foam?
steps.tip: Smell the warm cup. That bread smell is the yeast at work.

levels.explore: Watch the three cups, and point to the one that foams the most.
levels.develop: Guess, then measure the foam in each cup at 5 and 10 minutes.
levels.extend: With a kitchen thermometer, test two more temperatures between warm and very hot, and find the warmest water that still foams.

steps.title: Feed it and catch the gas
steps.why: Seeing the gas fill a balloon makes the invisible visible.
steps.kid: Your kid fills three bottles with warm water and yeast: one plain, one with sugar, one with sugar and salt. They stretch a balloon over each, using the Balloon test card, and measure each balloon with a string every 15 minutes.
steps.you: Help with the balloons. Ask them to predict which will grow biggest, and why salt might matter.
ask: What did the salt do to the yeast?
steps.tip: No balloons? Use three clear glasses and mark the foam line with tape every 15 minutes.

levels.explore: Watch the balloons, and say which one is biggest.
levels.develop: Measure each balloon every 15 minutes, and make a table.
levels.extend: Add a fourth bottle with a change you choose, like honey or flour instead of sugar, and test it.

steps.title: Mix and knead
steps.why: Kneading builds the stretchy strands that trap the gas.
steps.kid: Your kid weighs the ingredients from the Basic loaf card, mixes them, then kneads for 10 minutes, using the Knead it card. They stop and do the window test: stretch a small piece of dough until light shines through without it tearing.
steps.you: Show one push, fold and turn, then let them take over. Take turns when arms get tired. Raw dough isn't for tasting, so save the taste test for the baked loaf.
ask: How does the dough feel now compared with the start?
Does it pass the window test yet?
steps.tip: Weigh everything. Grams are more exact than cups, and it's easier to scale later.

levels.explore: Help pour and mix, then knead for as long as you can.
levels.develop: Weigh, mix and knead until the dough passes the window test.
levels.extend: Keep a small ball of dough unkneaded, bake it beside the loaf, and compare the inside.

steps.title: Watch it rise
steps.why: Measuring the rise turns waiting into data.
steps.kid: Your kid puts a walnut-sized piece of dough in a tall straight glass, presses it flat and marks the top with tape. They set the bowl and the glass in a warm spot and measure the height in the glass every 20 minutes, using the Rise watch card, until it doubles.
steps.you: Help find a warm spot, away from drafts. Set a timer so they remember to measure.
ask: How long did it take to double?
steps.tip: The glass shows what the big bowl is doing, in a way they can measure with a ruler.

levels.explore: Look at the tape mark, and say if the dough has grown.
levels.develop: Measure every 20 minutes, and draw a line graph of the rise.
levels.extend: Put a second glass somewhere cooler, and compare how fast each one rises.

steps.title: Bake it and scale it
steps.why: A real loaf is the reward, and baker's math is how bakers make any size they need.
steps.kid: Your kid shapes the loaf, lets it rise again, then watches you bake it. Once it's cool, they slice it and look at the holes the gas made. Then they use the Baker's math card to scale the recipe for a bigger loaf, or for a loaf to give away.
steps.you: Handle the oven. Ask them to tap the bottom of the loaf and listen for the hollow sound that means it's done.
ask: How much water would you need for 750 grams of flour?
steps.tip: Let it cool before slicing. It's still baking inside for a few minutes after it comes out.

levels.explore: Tap the loaf, and look at the holes inside with a magnifying glass or up close.
levels.develop: Scale the recipe to 750 grams of flour with baker's percentages.
levels.extend: Design your own loaf by changing one percentage, like more water, and bake it to test your idea.

reference.title: Bread Lab Toolkit
reference.intro: The tests, the recipe, how to knead and the math bakers use.

items.name: Yeast test

lines.v: 1 tsp yeast, a pinch of sugar, 100 ml water
from the kettle, poured by a grown-up

items.ask: Which cup did what you guessed?

items.name: Balloon test

lines.v: 1 tsp yeast and half a cup of warm water
plus 1 tbsp sugar and 1 tsp salt
string around each balloon, every 15 minutes

items.ask: What does yeast need to make the most gas?

items.name: Basic loaf

lines.v: 220°C (425°F), about 30 minutes, until it sounds hollow

items.ask: Which ingredient is the only living one?

items.name: Knead it

lines.v: away with the heel of your hand
stretches thin enough to see light; if it tears, knead 2 more minutes

items.ask: How did the dough change while you kneaded?

items.name: Rise watch

lines.v: a walnut of dough, pressed flat
when it has doubled, often 1 to 2 hours

items.ask: Did it rise at the same speed the whole time?

items.name: Baker's math

lines.v: 750 g flour needs 487.5 g water, 15 g salt, 10.5 g yeast

items.ask: Why do bakers start every recipe from the flour?

conclusion.headline: They baked a loaf and know why it rose.
conclusion.text: Give them the next loaf with no recipe card, only the baker's percentages. Whether they weigh the flour first and work out the rest says more about what stuck than the bread itself.
conclusion.celebrate: When they slice the first loaf, say: 'You woke up the yeast, fed it, and built the bread that caught its bubbles. You made that.'
extensions: Make pizza dough with the same baker's math, and change only the water
Bake a loaf for a neighbour or a friend, and write the recipe card to go with it
Find out how bread is made in another country, like tortillas, naan or pita, and what's different
Start a sourdough starter with flour and water only, and feed it for a week to catch wild yeast

signs: They talk about yeast as something alive
They weigh ingredients instead of guessing
They know why a loaf came out flat
makeItReal: Pick one slow morning this week, put flour, salt and yeast on the counter, and let your kid wake the yeast before you do anything else.
